source.title: Geometric invariants for real quadratic fields
source.authors: W. Duke, Ö. Imamoḡlu, Á. Tóth
source.version: Publisher final PDF, 42 pages; all printed pages 949–990 read, including Appendix A and references.

summary: To a narrow ideal class of a real quadratic field the paper attaches a hyperbolic surface bounded by the modular closed geodesic, with area πℓ_A. It proves equidistribution of these surfaces over a genus (Theorem 2) through extended Hecke and Katok–Sarnak formulas (Theorems 3–4). Reviewed by REV-PAPER-DUKE-IMAMOGLU-TOTH-16 (Claude Code, cc-2aeb03) and corrected in place: 188 items (16 library, 6 planned, 166 missing). 34 mistakes are recorded (21 misprints, 5 gaps, 8 errors; 3 reach a stated result, 6 a proof). With the corrections, Theorems 1–4 stand: Theorem 4's form F is unique only up to a unit (E2), and Proposition 2's bound (6.6) is false as printed and holds for the unit vector (E6), which is what Theorem 2 uses. Not formalised.

items.name: Reduction and complete class invariant
items.statement: Each A ∈ Cl+(K) contains fractional ideals wZ+Z (equal to, not merely proportional to) with w ∈ K and w > w^σ. The minus continued fraction of any such w is eventually periodic. Its primitive cycle ((n_1,…,n_ℓ)) is defined up to cyclic permutation and does not depend on the admissible choice of w. The expansion is purely periodic if and only if w is reduced (0 < w^σ < 1 < w) (cited: [28], [57]). The cycle is a complete invariant of A, and ℓ = ℓ_A equals the number of distinct reduced w with wZ+Z ∈ A.

items.name: Ideal to oriented form correspondence
items.statement: Let D be a fundamental discriminant. Narrow ideal classes of K correspond bijectively to PSL(2,Z)-classes of (necessarily primitive) forms [a,b,c] of discriminant D. The map sends 𝔞 = wZ+Z with w^σ < w to Q(x,y) = N(x − wy)/N(𝔞), taking the narrow class of 𝔞 to the Γ-class of Q. The inverse sends Q to wZ+Z with w = (−b+√D)/(2a), after choosing Q in its class with a > 0. If Q = [a,b,c] represents A, then (2.3) [a,−b,c] represents A^{-1}, (2.4) [−a,b,−c] represents JA, and (2.5) [−a,−b,−c] represents JA^{-1}.

items.name: Full-order Pell automorph
items.statement: For a primitive form Q=[a₀,b₀,c₀] with nonsquare discriminant d₀>1, let (t,u) be the smallest solution with t,u≥1 of t²−d₀u²=4. Then the group of automorphs of Q in Γ is generated by γ_Q=±[[(t−b₀u)/2, −c₀u],[a₀u, (t+b₀u)/2]] (2.11). If Q(x,y)=N(x−wy)/N(𝔞) comes from a narrow class of the fundamental discriminant D, then γ_Q=γ_w and ε_D=(t+u√D)/2. The attracting fixed point of γ_Q is (−b₀+√d₀)/(2a₀), so γ_Q moves points along S_Q clockwise when a₀>0 (counterclockwise when a₀<0). In §9, C_{nQ}=C_Q for n∈ℤ⁺.

items.statement: Let Γ be nonelementary with limit set Λ. Then R̂ − Λ is a countable union of disjoint open intervals. items.name: Oriented axis and closed geodesic
items.statement: Let A ∈ Cl+(K) and 𝔞 = wZ+Z ∈ A with w > w^σ (w need not be reduced). Let S_w be the geodesic in H with endpoints w^σ and w. Define γ_w = ±(a b; c d) ∈ Γ by (2.9): ε_D w = aw + b, ε_D = cw + d. Then γ_w is a primitive hyperbolic element of Γ with fixed points w^σ and w. The point w is attracting because (cw+d)^{-2} = ε_D^{-2} < 1, which gives S_w its clockwise orientation from w^σ to w. Different 𝔞 and w for A give Γ-conjugate γ_w. For z_0 ∈ S_w, the directed arc from z_0 to γ_w(z_0), reduced modulo Γ, is the closed geodesic C_A on Γ\H. It is well defined for A and gives a unique set of oriented, possibly overlapping arcs in F, also written C_A.

items.name: Fundamental polygon with free sides
items.statement: Fix the reduced w with cycle (n_1,…,n_ℓ) and set N_k = n_1+⋯+n_k (N_0 = 0, N_ℓ = m). The polygon P_A = {z ∈ H : 0 ≤ Re z ≤ m, |z − N_k| ≥ 1 for k = 0,…,ℓ} is a fundamental domain for Γ_A (Figures 1 and 4). The side pairings are: T^m pairs the vertical sides Re z = 0 and Re z = m; T^mS pairs the quarter-arcs of |z| = 1 and |z − m| = 1; and for 1 ≤ k ≤ ℓ−1, the semicircle |z − N_k| = 1 is split at the order-2 fixed point N_k + i and S_k pairs its two halves. The free sides are the real intervals [N_{k−1}+1, N_k−1] for k = 1,…,ℓ; when n_k = 2 such an interval degenerates to a tangency point. F_A is identified with P_A intersected with the region above the arcs of the geodesics S_{w_k} (endpoints w_k^σ, w_k) lying between the circles centred at N_{k−1} and N_k (p. 959).

items.statement: (p.969.) Let φ be an odd Hecke–Maass cusp form, so φ(−z̄) = −φ(z). Then Weyl(⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ) = 0 for every genus character χ, in all three cases of (5.12). By (2.2) the cycle of A^{−1} is that of A reversed, so T^{−m_A}F_{A^{−1}} is the mirror image of F_A (using the fundamental domains of Theorem 1). This gives (6.8): ∫_{F_{A^{−1}}} φ dμ = −∫_{F_A} φ dμ when d', d < 0. For d', d > 0 (boundary geodesics) and for d'd < 0 (CM points) the same cancellation follows from (2.3): [a, −b, c] represents A^{−1}, so S_{w'} = −S̄_w and z_{A^{−1}} = −z̄_A.

items.name: Core Stokes identity
items.statement: Lemma 2 (p.972). Let F be a real-analytic Γ_A-invariant function on H with ΔF = −y²(F_xx + F_yy) = s(1−s)F (7.10), and with ∫_0^m ∂_zF(x+iY)dx = o(1) as Y → ∞, where m = m_A is as in (2.1). Then (s(1−s)/2)∫_{F_A} F dμ = ∫_{∂F_A} i∂_zF(z)dz (7.11). Here ∫_{F_A} means lim_{Y→∞} of the integral over F_A(Y) = {z ∈ F_A : Im z < Y}, and ∂F_A is oriented like C_A (from w^σ towards w), so that F_A lies on its left. Lemma 1 (p.972, (7.9)). For u = E(z,s) with Re(s) = 1/2 and λ = s(1−s), and for u = ⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ with λ = 1/4 + r²: (λ/2)∫_{F_A} u dμ = ∫_{C_A} i∂_zu(z)dz. The integral over C_A runs along S_w from z_0 to γ_w(z_0) and does not depend on z_0.

items.name: Cusp decay for the Stokes input
items.statement: For u=E(z,1/2+it), its derivative constant terms are O(Y^(−1/2)) for fixed t, with the t=0 limit treated separately; nonconstant terms decay exponentially. Cusp forms have exponential decay. Hence the horizontal derivative integral tends to0 and u is absolutely integrable on each finite-width core cusp.

items.name: Genus Hecke factorization
items.statement: (p.971.) Let D = d'd be a fundamental discriminant, with d' and d fundamental discriminants (hence coprime), K = Q(√D), and χ the associated genus character of Cl^+(K). For D > 0, χ(J) = sign d = sign d'. Kronecker's decomposition holds: L(s,χ) = L(s,χ_{d'})L(s,χ_d). Equivalently Λ(s,χ) = Λ(s,χ_{d'})Λ(s,χ_d), with Λ(s,χ) as in (7.4)–(7.5) and Λ(s,χ_d) as in (5.13).

items.name: Correctly normalized cuspidal Weyl estimate
items.statement: Corrected form of (6.6) (see E6). For a Hecke–Maass cusp form φ of Laplace eigenvalue 1/4 + r², normalised by a(1) = 1 as in (5.7), and u_φ = φ/‖φ‖: Weyl(u_φ, χ) ≪_ε (1+r)^C |D|^{13/28+ε}. Equivalently, what Theorem 4 and [12, Thm. 5] give is Weyl(⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ, χ) ≪_ε (1+r)^C cosh²(πr/4) |D|^{13/28+ε} (13/28 = 3/4 − 2/7). The printed (6.6) has no factor cosh²(πr/4) and is false.
items.note: Not in the paper as stated: (6.6) is printed without the factor cosh²(πr/4) (E6). The two forms agree because ‖φ‖² = 2L(1,sym²φ)/cosh(πr) (Rankin–Selberg with the normalisations (5.2), (5.7), (5.8)) and L(1,sym²φ) ≪_ε r^ε. In the deduction of Theorem 2 the product c(φ)⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ = ⟨f,u_φ⟩u_φ is what enters, with ⟨f,u_φ⟩ ≪ r^{−A}, so the exponential factors cancel.

items.name: Smooth genus equidistribution
items.statement: (The step 'Theorem 2 follows from Propositions 1 and 2 and …', p.969, for smooth f.) Let f be a smooth, compactly supported Γ-invariant function and ε > 0. For every positive fundamental D and every genus G_D: Σ_{A∈G_D} ∫_{F_A} f dμ = (3/π)(∫_F f dμ)·Σ_{A∈G_D} area(F_A) + O_{f,ε}(D^{13/28+ε}). With Proposition 1 it follows that the ratio (Σ_{A∈G_D} ∫_{F_A} f dμ)/(Σ_{A∈G_D} area(F_A)) tends to (3/π)∫_F f dμ as D → ∞. The proof uses genus-character projection; the vanishing of surface Weyl sums for d', d > 0; odd cancellation (item 71); (6.5); the corrected unit-vector form of (6.6) (items 150–152); item 68; and Weyl's law (5.10).

items.name: Endpoint-justified integration by parts for both signs
items.statement: Under164, f_ε(t)=t^sH_ε(t) satisfies f_ε″+(1−s(s−1)/t²)f_ε=0 for every t>0 and ε=±1. Boundary terms in the θ integration by parts vanish, including for complex μ,s and 0<Re(s)≤1.
items.locator: Appendix A, proof of (A.1), p. 984: the displays from 'Using this last equation gives for the integral in (A.1)' to 'This proves that both sides of (A.1) satisfy the same differential equation', including the boundary term [e^{i(t cos θ+μθ)}M_{μ,λ}(2t sin θ)]_0^π = 0
proofSteps: Differentiate under the integral using164. For h=e^(εit cosθ)M(2t sinθ), the equation in163 gives L_t h=(2sin²θ−2μsinθ/t)h+4εi cosθ sinθ e^(εit cosθ)M′(2t sinθ), where L_t=d²/dt²+1−s(s−1)/t².
After multiplying by e^(εiμθ)/sinθ, the derivative term is (2εi/t)∫e^(εi(t cosθ+μθ))∂θM(2t sinθ)dθ.
Integrate first on [δ,π−δ]. By163 the endpoint terms are O(δ^σ); ∂θM is O(sin^(σ−1)θ), which is integrable. Thus the cutoff identity passes to the limit.
The derivative of the exponential is εi(−t sinθ+μ) times itself. Integration by parts converts the derivative term to ∫(−2sinθ+2μ/t)e^(εi(t cosθ+μθ))M dθ, cancelling the other two terms exactly.
The calculation uses ε²=1 and proves both signs directly. It does not assume M is real when μ,s are complex.

items.name: Exact conjugation of the two U and W normalizations
items.statement: On functions on H let C f(z)=Im(z)^(1/4)f(z), U₄f(z)=¼Σ_{ν mod4}f((z+ν)/4), W₄f(z)=(2z/i)^(−1/2)f(−1/(4z)) with the principal square root. Then CU₄C⁻¹=U and CW₄C⁻¹=W for the U,W displayed in DIT16 p976, and C(U₄∘W₄)C⁻¹=U∘W. This calculation alone does not identify U∘W with W∘U on the automorphic subspace.
items.locator: DIT11 p. 959, the unnumbered display defining U₄ and W₄ (after 'pr⁺ = ⅔(U₄∘W₄)+⅓', before (2.19)); DIT16 p. 976, the definitions of U and W and footnote 6
proofSteps: Im((z+ν)/4)=y/4, so conjugation contributes4^(1/4)=√2 to U₄'s scalar1/4.
Im(−1/(4z))=y/(4|z|²). The absolute scalar from C and C⁻¹ is√(2|z|), cancelling that of (2z/i)^(−1/2). For arg z∈(0,π), arg(z/i)=arg z−π/2 is principal, leaving e^(iπ/4)(z/|z|)^(−1/2).

Conjugation preserves composition order. DIT11 explicitly prints U₄∘W₄; DIT16 prints WU. Resolving a possible action convention or proving equality on the appropriate automorphic space remains S5. No counterexample on arbitrary nonautomorphic functions is asserted to refute a projection theorem.
Read this historical open-order statement together with176/180: the new proof fixes the DIT16 convention, without asserting UW=WU on a restricted cuspidal space.

items.name: Finite Fourier certificate with conjugated trace coefficients
items.statement: For an orthonormal basis f₁,…,f_m of W₁, there exist m positive admissible indices n_i for which the matrix (conj(b_{f_j}(n_i))) is invertible. This uses all positive admissible coefficients, not only fundamental indices.

proofSteps: The restrictions b_n|W₁ have common kernel W₀∩W₁=0. By170 they span W₁*, and finite dimensionality selects a basis of m such forms.
Complex conjugation preserves invertibility. Equivalently a row relation Σα_j conj(b_j(n))=0 conjugates to b_{Σconj(α_j)f_j}(n)=0, forcing all α_j=0.
The empty matrix handles m=0. This argument supplies no nonzero fundamental coefficient and no injectivity of the lift.

items.name: Automorphy from finite Fourier separation
items.statement: Assume the convergent Biró lift and identity183 for every positive admissible n. Then each Sh_D f is a level-one weight-zero cusp eigenform at parameter r (possibly zero), for every f∈W. If D>0 the coefficient formula is even in the Fourier index, so the lift is even.
items.locator: Biró, Theorem 1, p. 106 (statement), proof on p. 129; DIT16 p. 982 cites 'the proof of Theorem 1 on page 129 of Biró' as the model argument
proofSteps: On W₀ the lift is identically zero by181.
On W₁ choose the invertible coefficient matrix from182. Divide each identity183 by its nonzero scalar12√π(Dn_i)^(3/4).
Invert the finite matrix. Each individual lift becomes a finite linear combination of cusp eigenforms, preserving automorphy, cuspidality and the same eigenvalue.
Linearity handles all f. The formula185 gives A_D(−n)=A_D(n). This proves neither nonzero image nor an eigenline bijection; negative-D inputs of DIT16 need the wider identity separately.

items.name: Sufficient condition for J ≠ I
items.statement: If D is divisible by a prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4), then J ≠ I, i.e. O_K has no unit of norm −1.
items.note: Proof: a unit of norm −1 gives x² − Dy² = −4, so −4 and hence −1 is a square mod p, which is impossible. Used on p. 960 (J is in the principal genus iff no prime p ≡ 3 mod 4 divides D) and in the D = 4p discussion. Missing: routed to route 10.

items.statement: F = {z ∈ H : −1/2 ≤ Re z ≤ 0 and |z| ≥ 1} ∪ {z ∈ H : 0 < Re z < 1/2 and |z| > 1}. This is an exact set of representatives for PSL(2,Z)\H.

items.statement: Γ = PSL(2,Z) is generated by S = ±(0 1; −1 0) and T = ±(1 1; 0 1), and has signature (0;2,3;1,0).

items.name: Surface F_Γ and the boundary convention ∂F_Γ
items.statement: For finitely generated Γ, let F_Γ ⊂ H be a fundamental domain for Γ\N_Γ, identified with the surface Γ\N_Γ (which has t geodesic boundary curves, s cusps and r orbifold points). ∂F_Γ denotes the preimage of the boundary of the surface, as a subset of the boundary of the fundamental domain. Sides of the closure of F_Γ that are identified by Γ are not counted as boundary.

items.name: Boundary circles are homotopic to unique closed geodesics bounding the Nielsen core (cited)
items.statement: Let Γ be finitely generated with signature (g;m_1,…,m_r;s;t), and let H* be H with the elliptic points of Γ removed. Then Γ\H* is a Riemann surface of genus g with t conformal disks and finitely many points removed. The positively oriented boundary circle of each removed disk is freely homotopic in Γ\H* to a unique closed geodesic, and these t geodesics form the boundary of the image in Γ\H* of the closure of N_Γ.

items.name: Γ_A has infinite index in PSL(2,Z)
items.statement: Γ_A is an infinite-index ('thin') subgroup of Γ = PSL(2,Z), and hence (being finitely generated) a Fuchsian group of the second kind.
items.note: Theorem 1 states only 'second kind'. Infinite index follows from it, because a finite-index subgroup of PSL(2,Z) has limit set R̂. Equally, the polygon has infinite area. The implication 'infinite index ⇒ second kind' used in the text needs finite generation (geometric finiteness). Missing: routed to route 9.

items.name: Cutting the axis arc into the boundary of F_A ((3.6), Figure 7)
items.statement: Let z be the intersection of |z| = 1 with S_w, which exists by (3.5), and let γ = γ_w. Then (3.6) T^{−m}S_ℓ⋯S_2S_1γ(z) = z. The arc of S_w from z to γ(z) is cut successively: its part between |z| = 1 and |z − N_1| = 1 is kept. S_1 maps the remainder onto part of S_{w_2}, whose part between |z − N_1| = 1 and |z − N_2| = 1 is kept, and so on up to S_ℓ. The ℓ kept arcs lie in the fundamental polygon, and under the side pairings S_k and (T^mS)^{-1} they close up into exactly one copy of C_A, of length 2 log ε_D. This closed geodesic is freely homotopic to the boundary circle of Γ_A\H*.
items.note: This is the proof device for item 37. (3.6) is a numbered display with no item. The last kept arc ends exactly on |z − m| = 1, at S_{ℓ−1}⋯S_1γ(z) = S_ℓT^m z = T^m S z (see new source issue 3). Missing: routed to route 9.

items.name: Vanishing of the Weyl integrals of the wrong sign
items.statement: Let D>0 be a fundamental discriminant, D=d′d a factorization into fundamental discriminants with genus character χ, and u either E(z,s) with Re(s)=1/2 or ⟨φ,φ⟩^{−1}φ for a Hecke–Maass cusp form φ (λ its eigenvalue). If d′,d>0 then Σ_{A∈Cl⁺(K)} χ(A)(λ/2)∫_{F_A}u dμ = 0 (this includes the trivial character d′=1). If d′,d<0 then Σ_{A∈Cl⁺(K)} χ(A)∫_{∂F_A}u y^{−1}|dz| = 0.
items.note: Asserted without proof ('This is enough since the Weyl integral in (5.12) in the first case is zero when d′,d>0 as is that in the second case when d′,d<0'). It is used in §6 to reduce Theorem 2 to the characters with d′,d<0 and (4.4) to those with d′,d>0. Proof: χ(JA^{−1})=χ(J)χ(A) with χ(J)=sign d; C_{JA^{−1}} is C_A reversed ((2.5), p954); for the length case the two arc-length integrals are equal and χ(J)=−1 makes them cancel, and A²=J is impossible when χ(J)=−1; for the area case use Lemma 1 (7.9), (λ/2)∫_{F_A}u dμ=∫_{C_A} i∂_z u dz, which changes sign under reversal while χ(J)=1 (a reciprocal C_A gives 0). Alternatively complementarity (item 49) plus ∫_F u dμ=0. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Absolute integrability of E(z,s) over F_A on the critical line
items.statement: For Re(s)=1/2, E(z,s) is absolutely integrable over F_A with respect to dμ=y^{−2}dxdy.
items.note: From (5.3): E(z,s)=y^s+φ(s)y^{1−s}+O(e^{−cy}) with |y^s|=|y^{1−s}|=y^{1/2}, and the cusp of F_A is a half-strip of width m_A, where ∫^∞ y^{1/2}y^{−2}dy<∞. Needed for the first branch of (5.12) and of Theorem 3 with u=E. Related to C138 (growth condition for Stokes) but distinct. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Coefficients of the weight-1/2 plus-space Eisenstein series (black box from [16])
items.statement: In the notation of DIT11 ([16]): for m∈Z⁺ and D a fundamental discriminant, Σ_{n|m}(D/n) b_0(Dm²/n², s) = 2^{2−4s}π^{s+1/4}m^{3/2−2s}|D|^{s−1/4}σ_{4s−2}(m)L_D(2s−1/2)/ζ(4s−1), and b_0(0,s)=π^{1/2}2^{5/2−6s}Γ(2s)ζ(4s−2)/ζ(4s−1), where b_0(n,s) are the Fourier coefficients of P⁺_0(τ,s) in [16, (2.20)–(2.21)]. Consequently E*_{1/2}(z,s) = 2^sΛ(2s) y^{1/4} P⁺_0(z, s/2+1/4) has the expansion displayed on DIT16 p964, with b(d,s)=(4π)^{−1/4}|d|^{−3/4}Λ(s,χ_d) for fundamental d and the stated Shimura relation.
items.locator: DIT11 Lemma 4, (2.23)–(2.25), pp961–962; used for the E*_{1/2} display, DIT16 p964, which cites only [16, Prop. 2 p. 959]
items.note: I checked that the DIT16 constant terms Λ(2s)2^s y^{s/2+1/4}, Λ(2−2s)2^{1−s}y^{3/4−s/2}, b(d,s) for both signs of d, and the Shimura relation with m^{s−1/2}σ_{1−2s}(m) all follow from (2.23)–(2.24) with s′=s/2+1/4, the unitary factor y^{1/4} and the constant 2^sΛ(2s). Not used in any proof of DIT16 (only in the heuristic remarks). Missing: routed to route 3.

items.name: First five level-one cuspidal eigenvalues (numerical, cited)
items.statement: The first five Laplace eigenvalues of Hecke–Maass cusp forms for PSL(2,Z) are 91.14134…, 148.43213…, 190.13154…, 206.41679…, 260.68740…; all belong to odd forms except the third (190.13154…), which belongs to an even form.
items.note: Numbered statement, not used in any proof; the values are truncated (not rounded) to five decimals (e.g. 1/4+13.7797513519²=190.1315473…). The third eigenvalue is the φ of the numerical examples on pp966–967. Missing: routed to route 4.

items.name: Eisenstein Weyl sums bounded by Dirichlet L-values
items.statement: There is an absolute C > 0 such that, for every ε > 0, every fundamental D = d'd with genus character χ, and every s with Re(s) = 1/2: Weyl(E(·,s),χ) ≪_ε |s|^C |L(s,χ_{d'})L(s,χ_d)| |D|^{1/4+ε}. The paper prints the left side as 'Weyl(s,χ)'.
items.note: This follows from Theorem 3. Weyl(E(·,s),χ) = Λ(2s)^{−1}Λ(s,χ_{d'})Λ(s,χ_d), divided by 2√π when d'd < 0, with Λ(2s) = π^{−s}Γ(s)ζ(2s). The gamma ratio is ≪ |s|^{1/2} by Stirling, and 1/|ζ(1+2it)| ≪ log(2+|t|). The |D|^ε is not needed. Uses the missing item gamma-quotient-and-zeta-one-line-bounds. Missing: routed to route 6.

items.name: Standard gamma-quotient and 1/ζ(1+2it) estimates (black box)
items.locator: Proof of Proposition 2, p.969 ('standard estimates for the gamma function quotient and for ζ(2s)')
items.note: Classical results, used as black boxes. Missing: routed to route 6.

items.name: Siegel's theorem (black box)
items.statement: For every ε > 0 there is c(ε) > 0, not effectively computable, such that L(1,χ_D) ≥ c(ε)|D|^{−ε} for every fundamental discriminant D ≠ 1.
items.locator: §6, p.968 ('By Siegel's theorem'); proof of Proposition 1, p.968 ('Siegel's theorem (see [11])')
items.note: Item 145 states only the consequences h(D) log ε_D ≫_ε D^{1/2−ε} and h(D) ≫_ε |D|^{1/2−ε}. Siegel's theorem itself is the black box and is the source of the ineffectivity in Proposition 1. Missing: routed to route 6.

items.name: Dirichlet's class number formula for quadratic fields (narrow form)
items.statement: For a fundamental discriminant D > 1, with h(D) = #Cl^+(K) the narrow class number and ε_D > 1 the least unit of norm +1: h(D) log ε_D = √D·L(1,χ_D). For a fundamental D < 0: h(D) = ω_D √|D| L(1,χ_D)/π, with ω_D as in (5.12).
items.locator: §6, p.967 ('by the class number formula'); used in the proof of Proposition 1, p.968
items.note: This is the form the paper uses. It follows from item 144 and ζ_K = ζ·L(s,χ_D). If N(ε_0) = −1 then h^+ = h and ε_D = ε_0². If N(ε_0) = +1 then h^+ = 2h and ε_D = ε_0. In both cases h^+ log ε_D = 2h log ε_0 = √D L(1,χ_D). Checks: D = −4 and D = −3 give h = 1; D = 5 gives h^+ = 1. Planned: AnalyticNumberTheory AN.4 plans Hecke characters, completed Hecke L-functions and the analytic class number formula.

items.name: Main terms for the geodesic and CM problems
items.statement: For a fundamental D > 1 and any genus G_D: Σ_{A∈G_D} length(∂F_A) = 2^{2−ω(D)} h(D) log ε_D. For a fundamental D < 0: #G_D = 2^{1−ω(D)} h(D). By the class number formula and Siegel's theorem, each is ≫_ε |D|^{1/2−ε} for every ε > 0, with an ineffective constant.
items.note: The first identity comes from (3.3) (length(∂F_A) = 2 log ε_D) and (4.2), not from the class number formula to which the text attributes it. The lower bound also uses 2^{ω(D)} ≪_ε |D|^ε. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Completed Hecke L-function of a narrow class character
items.statement: For a character χ of Cl^+(K), K = Q(√D) with D fundamental: if D < 0, Λ(s,χ) = π^{−s}Γ(s/2)Γ((s+1)/2)|D|^{s/2}L(s,χ) = 2^{1−s}π^{1/2−s}|D|^{s/2}Γ(s)L(s,χ) (7.4). If D > 0, Λ(s,χ) = π^{−s}Γ((s+α)/2)²D^{s/2}L(s,χ), with α = α_χ = (1 − χ(J))/2 (7.5).
items.note: The second equality in (7.4) is the duplication formula; I checked it. Item 134 defines only L(s,χ). Planned: AnalyticNumberTheory AN.4 plans Hecke characters, completed Hecke L-functions and the analytic class number formula.

items.name: Hecke's formulas for Λ(s,χ), continuation and functional equation
items.statement: Let χ be any character of Cl^+(K), K = Q(√D) with D fundamental. If D < 0: Λ(s,χ) = (2√π/ω_D)Σ_{A∈Cl^+(K)} χ(A)E*(z_A,s) (7.6). If D > 0: Λ(s,χ) = Σ_{A∈Cl^+(K)} χ(A)∫_{C_A} E*(z,s)y^{−1}|dz| when χ(J) = 1, and Σ_{A∈Cl^+(K)} χ(A)∫_{C_A} i∂_zE*(z,s)dz when χ(J) = −1 (7.7). Consequently Λ(s,χ) continues meromorphically to C, with at most simple poles at s = 0, 1, and by (5.4) it satisfies Λ(1−s,χ) = Λ(s,χ).
items.note: (7.6) follows from (7.1) and (7.4). (7.7) follows from (7.2)/(7.3), because χ(JA) = χ(J)χ(A) gives Σ_Aχ(A)ζ_A = ½Σ_Aχ(A)(ζ_A ± ζ_{JA}). I checked (7.1)–(7.3) independently by unfolding, including the sign in (7.3) for the paper's orientation of C_A (from w^σ towards w). Items 140–142 are the genus-character specializations. Planned: AnalyticNumberTheory AN.4 plans Hecke characters, completed Hecke L-functions and the analytic class number formula.

items.name: Integral over the closed geodesic C_A
items.statement: For a Γ-invariant function or 1-form, the integral over C_A is the integral along the geodesic S_w, oriented from w^σ towards w, from any z_0 ∈ S_w to γ_w(z_0) ∈ S_w. It is assumed (and holds for Γ-invariant integrands) that the value does not depend on z_0.
items.note: This convention is used in (7.2), (7.3), (7.7), (7.8) and Lemma 1. Item A24 constructs C_A but does not fix the integral. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Oriented cycle C_Q of an indefinite form (§9)
items.statement: Let D>0 be nonsquare and Q=[a,b,c] a primitive form of discriminant D. Let S_Q={z∈H: a|z|²+b Re z+c=0} and z∈S_Q. C_Q is the directed arc of S_Q from z to γ_Qz, with γ_Q as in (2.11), and C_{nQ}=C_Q for n∈ℤ⁺. For a Γ-invariant function or 1-form, ∫_{C_Q} does not depend on z and depends only on the Γ-class of Q. The orientation is clockwise on S_Q when a>0, the same as C_A in §2. By footnote 8, DIT11 [16] used g_Q=γ_Q⁻¹, i.e. the opposite orientation.
items.note: Lemmas 5 and 6 differ in sign unless this orientation is fixed; see the new source issue. The orientation stated here is the one under which Lemma 5, Proposition 5, Proposition 6 and the passage to Theorem 4 through Lemma 1 are correct. The paper's wording ('define C_{nQ}=C_Q as in [16] using (2.11)', and footnote 8) leaves the orientation implicit. Missing: routed to route 1.

items.name: Geometric trace T(φ,χ)
items.statement: Let φ be a Hecke–Maass cusp form, d fundamental, d′ a discriminant with D=d′d nonsquare, and χ the genus character of D=d′d. Then T(φ,χ)=⟨φ,φ⟩⁻¹Σ_{Q∈Γ\Q_D}χ(Q)·Y_Q, where Y_Q=2√πω_Q⁻¹φ(z_Q) if d′d<0, Y_Q=∫_{C_Q}φ(z)y⁻¹|dz| if d′,d>0, and Y_Q=∫_{C_Q}i∂_zφ(z)dz if d′,d<0, with C_Q oriented as in the item above.
items.note: Items 124 and 127 use T without an item that defines it. For odd φ, T(φ,χ)=0 (use Q↦[a,−b,c]); in the proof this falls out of the final linear-independence step. Missing: routed to route 3.

items.name: Fourier expansion of F_m(z,s) (cited)
items.statement: Let m≠0 and Re(s)>1. Then F_m(z,s)=f_m(z,s)+2|m|^{1/2−s}σ_{2s−1}(|m|)((2s−1)Λ(2s))⁻¹y^{1−s}+2y^{1/2}Σ_{n≠0}Φ(m,n;s)K_{s−1/2}(2π|n|y)e(nx), with Λ(s)=π^{−s/2}Γ(s/2)ζ(s) and Φ as in item 88.
items.note: The paper prints a stray ']' after y^{1−s}. I checked the constant term and the n-th coefficient integrals numerically ((m,s,y)=(1,3,0.7),(2,2.5,0.9); (m,n) including n=−4): DIT16's formula is correct. The cited DIT11 p.970 expansion of G_m=2π|m|^{1/2}F_m has an extra factor |n|^{1/2} in the n-th coefficient; that is DIT11's misprint, not DIT16's. Items 93 and 94 need this expansion. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Fourier expansion of the weight-0 resolvent kernel (Fay Thm 3.1, cited)
items.statement: Let Re(s)>1 and let y′>max_{γ∈Γ}Im(γz), which holds for example when z lies in the standard fundamental domain and y′>y. Then G(z,z′;s)=(2s−1)⁻¹y′^{1−s}E(z,s)+√y′Σ_{m≠0}F_{−m}(z,s)K_{s−1/2}(2π|m|y′)e(mx′).
items.note: The paper writes the sum over all m∈ℤ, where the m=0 term K_{s−1/2}(0) is meaningless, and states validity for y′>y (see the new source issue). The m=0 term above is the m→0 limit of the general term. This expansion is the black box behind Proposition 3. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Fourier expansion and residues of the weight-1/2 resolvent (Fay, cited)
items.statement: Let Re(s)>1 and Im z′>Im z, with z in reduced position. Then G_{1/2}(z′,z;s)=Σ_{n≠0}F_{1/2,n}(z,s)W_{sgn(n)/4,s−1/2}(4π|n|y′)e(−nx′) plus the n=0 (Eisenstein) term, with F_{1/2,n} as in (8.6). G_{1/2} continues meromorphically in s, and Res_{s=1/2+ir/2}(2s−1)G_{1/2}(z′,z;s)=Σ_ψ conj(ψ(z′))ψ(z) over an orthonormal basis of V_r. By Fay [20, Cor. 3.6, p.178], Φ⁺(n,d;s) continues meromorphically to all s.
items.locator: §8, pp.975–977, citing Fay [20, Thm 3.1] and footnote 5; Fay Cor. 3.6 p.178
items.note: Items 95 and 97 state the construction and the residue of F_{1/2,n}, but not the expansion from which (8.7) is read off. As a consistency check, the weight-0 specialisation of the (8.6) normalisation, Γ(s)/(4π|n|Γ(2s))M_{0,s−1/2}(4π|n|y)=f_n/(2|n|^{1/2}), reproduces (8.3), because √y′K_{s−1/2}(2π|n|y′)=W_{0,s−1/2}(4π|n|y′)/(2|n|^{1/2}). Missing: routed to route 3.

items.name: Shimura Dirichlet-series identity for ψ∈B_r
items.statement: Let ψ∈B_r have coefficients b(n) as in (10.1), and let d be a fundamental discriminant. Then L_d(s+1/2)Σ_{n≥1}b(dn²)n^{1−s}=b(d)Π_p(1−a_ψ(p)p^{−s}+p^{−2s})⁻¹, where L_d(s)=L(s,χ_d)=Σ_{n≥1}(d/n)n^{−s} and a_ψ(p) is the T_{p²}-eigenvalue. Comparing coefficients gives mΣ_{n|m}n^{−3/2}(d/n)b(m²d/n²)=a_ψ(m)b(d) (item 122).
items.note: The paper does not define L_d. The Euler product runs over all p, including p=2, while B_r is only asserted to diagonalise T_{p²} for p>2 (see the new gap). I checked the coefficient extraction. Missing: routed to route 3.

items.name: Series expansion (A.2) of the Whittaker cycle integral
items.statement: For μ ∈ ℂ, Re(s) > 0 and t > 0, ∫_0^π e^{i(t cos θ+μθ)} M_{μ,s−1/2}(2t sin θ) dθ/sin θ = 2π e(μ/4) Γ(2s) Σ_{ℓ≥0} Σ_{m+n=ℓ} (−1)^m (s−μ)_n Γ(s+n) / ( m! n! Γ(2s+n) Γ((n+s+m+μ+1)/2) Γ((n+s−m−μ+1)/2) ) · t^{s+ℓ}. The double series converges absolutely for every t, and the reciprocal gammas are entire. The paper writes (s−μ)_n as Γ(s−μ+n)/Γ(s−μ), so the printed prefactor is 2π e(μ/4)Γ(2s)/Γ(s−μ).
items.note: Obtained by inserting the series of M (item 112) and e^{it cos θ − t sin θ} = Σ_m (it)^m e^{imθ}/m!, then integrating termwise with the corrected formula of item 115 (ν = n+s, β = m+μ). The factor 2^{n+s−1} of the corrected formula cancels (2t)^{n+s}. Correct as printed. I checked it numerically against (A.3) through t^{s+5}. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Series expansion (A.3) of G(s,μ) t^{1/2} J_{s−1/2}(t)
items.note: Correct as printed. It follows from t^{1/2}J_{s−1/2}(t) = √2 Σ (−1)^r (t/2)^{s+2r}/(r!Γ(s+1/2+r)); the display before (A.3) omits the √2 (E10). Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Bessel's equation and the ODE for t^{1/2}J_λ
items.statement: For λ ∈ ℂ and t > 0, J_λ satisfies t²J_λ″ + tJ_λ′ + (t²−λ²)J_λ = 0. Hence g(t) = t^{1/2}J_λ(t) satisfies t^{3/2}[g″(t) + (1 + (1/4−λ²)/t²) g(t)] = t²J_λ″ + tJ_λ′ + (t²−λ²)J_λ = 0. With λ = s−1/2, g solves f″ + (1 − s(s−1)/t²) f = 0.
items.locator: Appendix A, proof of (A.1), p. 983 ('A simple computation shows that …')
items.note: A standard fact used as a black box (refs [38], [55]). The identity t^{3/2}(…) = t²J″+tJ′+(t²−λ²)J checks directly. No existing item covers the Bessel ODE; item 111 has only the series definitions. Missing: routed to route 2.

items.name: Agreement of the first coefficients of (A.2) and (A.3)
items.statement: In (A.2) and (A.3) the coefficients of t^s agree, both being 2π e(μ/4) Γ(s) / (Γ((s+1+μ)/2) Γ((s+1−μ)/2)). The coefficient of t^{s+1} in (A.2) is 0: the terms (m,n) = (1,0) and (0,1) cancel because ((s−μ)/2)/Γ((s−μ)/2+1) = 1/Γ((s−μ)/2). The coefficients of t^{s+2} also agree. Together with the common ODE and Frobenius uniqueness (the step recorded in E11: a solution t^s Σ c_n t^n of the ODE is determined by c_0), this proves (A.1).
items.locator: Appendix A, p. 985 (last paragraph of the proof)
items.note: The paper says only 'A straightforward calculation shows …'. The t^s match uses the duplication formula Γ(2s) = 2^{2s−1}π^{−1/2}Γ(s)Γ(s+1/2). I verified numerically that all coefficients up to t^{s+5} agree. Only the t^s coefficient is needed, as the paper remarks. Missing: routed to route 2.

routes.reason: Reduction of integral quadratic forms, their oriented geodesics and Duke-type distribution are explicitly in GN.3–4. Import the core surface from FuchsianOrbifoldsPartII and genus algebra from MultiquadraticPartII; use MP.7 traces and AS spectral estimates. Do not duplicate the core construction or generic functional analysis.

The noncompact Laplacian, Eisenstein/Poincaré families, resolvent residues, Bessel suppliers and spectral expansion belong to the existing spectral layers. AS.0 supplies analytic operators and special-function interfaces, AS.1 initial convergence, AS.2 continuation, and AS.4 modular spectrum and summation. MP.7 imports these and supplies multiplier-specific adaptations. Continuation suppliers162–167 import the already built regularized hypergeometric series, beta/gamma identities and dominated differentiation (159–161); only the specific adapters, endpoint estimates and cycle integral proof are routed, not generic convergence/integration machinery. QSeriesPartitionsAndMockModularForms:QM.2 may reuse the Bessel adapter rather than redeclare it. The Biró interior convergence repair187 imports the already built TauCeti Vitali theorem171. Boundary-residue guard188 prevents this import from being used as an unproved uniform estimate.

The existing half-integral-weight stage owns theta multipliers, plus-space projection, half-weight Fourier/Kloosterman coefficients, Shimura eigenlines and coefficient traces. MP.5 supplies theta kernels and their norms. Import generic resolvents/Bessel analysis from AS and central-value period identities from GZ.5. No genus-two MP.8 extension is needed. Continuation175–186 are the specific level-four coset, cusp, finite-Fourier and normalization adapters. Import170–174 rather than replan duality, Vitali, theta, j or GL₂ multiplicity one. review.reason: The quotation matches p. 952. The paragraph is set up for an arbitrary nonelementary Fuchsian Γ ⊂ PSL(2,R) with no normalisation. The limit set Λ is a closed subset of ℝ̂ = ℝ ∪ {∞}, so 'Λ = ℝ' should read 'Λ = ℝ̂'. The description 'open half-planes that lie above the geodesics' gives the Nielsen region (Beardon [2, §8.5]: the side of each geodesic away from its interval of discontinuity) only when every component of ℝ̂ − Λ is a bounded interval of ℝ. That means ∞ ∈ Λ and Λ unbounded in both directions. Two cases fail. (a) If ∞ ∉ Λ, the component containing ∞ appears in ℝ − Λ as two rays (−∞,a) and (b,∞). Their geodesics are vertical lines, so 'above' makes no sense, and the correct half-plane is the inside of the semicircle from a to b. (b) If ∞ ∈ Λ but Λ ∩ ℝ is bounded above (or below), there is a ray (b,∞) whose geodesic is the line Re z = b. In either case the literal definition does not give the Γ-invariant hull that the next sentence cites from [2, Thm. 8.5.2]. The defence holds, so affects = nothing is right. Every group the paper uses (PSL(2,Z), and each Γ_A, which contains T^m) has Λ invariant under a translation. So ∞ ∈ Λ, Λ is unbounded both ways, all intervals are bounded, and 'above' is correct. The intended object (the Nielsen region, named and cited) is unambiguous, so the classification as a misprint or imprecision is fair.

sourceIssues.printed: "By the above construction of F_A, each elliptic fixed point in F_A determines a unique point on the boundary geodesic that is closest to it. ... Using (2.7) we compute the cycle of hyperbolic distances between successive fixed points of S_0, S_1, … S_ℓ in H. This is given by (V(n_1), V(n_2), … V(n_ℓ)) ... sourceIssues.correction: Replace the last paragraph of the proof with the following. A conformal equivalence F_A → F_B, of Riemann orbifolds with their cone points of order 2, is an isometry (pass to the doubles and use uniqueness of the hyperbolic structure). It therefore lifts to φ ∈ PSL(2,R) with φΓ_Aφ^{−1} = Γ_B. Composing with an element of Γ_B (one cusp class), we may take φ(∞) = ∞, so φ(z) = az + b with a > 0. Since Γ_A ⊂ PSL(2,Z), Im γ(N_k + i) = 1/((cN_k+d)² + c²) ≤ 1, with equality exactly for γ ∈ T^{mZ} ∪ T^{mZ}S_k. So the points of maximal height in the ℓ elliptic orbits of Γ_A are N_k + mZ + i, k = 1,…,ℓ, and likewise for Γ_B. Hence a = 1 and the two sets correspond under a translation. Their successive gaps (n_1,…,n_ℓ) therefore agree up to cyclic rotation, and the cycle is a complete invariant of A. Alternatively, keep the distance argument, but prove that the nearest boundary point is unique and gives the stated order. Then define the k-th length intrinsically, as the length of the geodesic arc from P_{k−1} to P_k homotopic to the path through the boundary between their feet, and show that this length is V(n_k). Also state in Theorem 1 that 'conformal class' is taken with the cone points.
sourceIssues.reason: A conformal equivalence F_A → F_B preserves only intrinsic data. Step (i) (uniqueness of the closest point and the resulting order) is stated without argument. The result itself is true, by the normalisation argument above, and V is correct and strictly increasing. So only the proof is incomplete.

review.reason: The quotations match p. 959. The proof rests on two things. First, an ordering of the cone points, via a 'unique' nearest boundary point, asserted from 'the above construction'. Second, the claim that the H-distances V(n_k) = d(N_{k−1}+i, N_k+i) between these particular lifts are preserved by conformal equivalence. A conformal (orbifold) equivalence F_A → F_B is an isometry. It preserves distances on the surface and lengths of intrinsically defined arcs, but not distances between arbitrarily chosen lifts in H. The V(n_k) are not surface distances in general. For ℓ = 1 the 'successive' fixed points i and n_1+i are the same point of F_A. For D = 28, class I (cycle (3,6)), F_I has two cone points, [i] = [9+i] and [3+i]. Their distance on F_I is at most V(3) ≈ 2.390, yet the proof's cycle is (V(3), V(6)) ≈ (2.390, 3.637). So V(6) is only the length of one particular geodesic arc, and the proof never characterises that arc intrinsically, for instance by a homotopy class tied to the boundary ordering. The uniqueness of the nearest boundary point and the claim that the induced order is N_0, N_1, …, N_{ℓ−1} are also unargued. So the step fails as written. The theorem is nevertheless true, and I checked the proposed repair. A conformal equivalence of the bordered orbifolds extends to the doubles, which carry unique complete hyperbolic orbifold metrics, so it is an isometry. It lifts to φ ∈ PSL(2,R) with φΓ_Aφ^{−1} = Γ_B. Each Γ_B has one cusp class, so after composing with an element of Γ_B we may assume φ(∞) = ∞, hence φ(z) = az + b with a > 0. For γ ∈ Γ_A ⊂ PSL(2,Z), Im γ(N_k+i) = 1/((cN_k+d)² + c²) ≤ 1. Equality holds only for (c,d) = ±(0,1), i.e. γ = T^j ∈ Γ_A so m | j (the cusp stabiliser is ⟨T^m⟩), or for (c,d) = ±(1,−N_k), i.e. γ = T^{j}S_k with m | j. So the highest points of the elliptic orbits are exactly N_k + mZ + i, all at height 1. φ scales heights by a, so a = 1, and {N'_j} ≡ {N_k} + b mod m. So the gap cycles agree up to rotation, and orientation is kept because φ preserves orientation. Since the cycle is a complete invariant (p. 951), B = A. V(x) = arccosh(1 + x²/2) is correct and strictly increasing, which I checked numerically for x = 2, 3, 6. A precision remark that does not change the verdict: the statement must be read with F_A as a Riemann orbifold, with its ℓ cone points of order 2 (and the cusp) as part of the structure. That is what the paper's 'contains ℓ points of order 2' and its use of hyperbolic distances intend. Forgetting the cone points, every F_A is conformally a punctured closed disc {0 < |z| ≤ 1}, so the bare conformal type carries no information.

Yet the displayed relation after (10.1), (10.2) and hence (10.3) use a_ψ(p) for every prime, including p=2, and the text never defines a_ψ(2). The a_ψ(2^k) enter (10.4) for even m, and so (10.6). Its natural proof, through the Shimura relation and the fact that every n≡0,1 mod 4 is dk², also needs the p=2 part, because the odd-p relations never reach b(4^k d). Case for the defence: Kohnen's plus-space Hecke operator at 2 and the Hecke-equivariant plus-space correspondence of [34]/[1], invoked at the end of the proof, supply what is missing, so Proposition 6 stands. As written, though, the construction is incomplete at p=2. (10.4) also uses silently that a_ψ(m) is real (T_{p²} is self-adjoint) when the Hecke relation is conjugated. That is harmless.

review.reason: Checked on a 300 dpi crop of p. 984. The first display prints '+ 2i sin 2θ e^{±i(t cos θ)} M′_{μ,λ}(2t sin θ)'. The proof has just restricted to the + signs (p. 983) and defined h(t) = e^{i(t cos θ)}M_{μ,λ}(2t sin θ). The cross term of h″ is 2·(i cos θ)(2 sin θ)e^{i t cos θ}M′ = 2i sin 2θ e^{i t cos θ}M′, so the exponent is +i t cos θ. The '±' cannot be read as covering both signs either: with h = e^{−i t cos θ}M the coefficient would become −2i, so a ± would be needed on the 2i as well. The rest of the display is correct. By the Whittaker equation, 4 sin²θ M″ = (sin²θ − 2μ sin θ/t − (1/4−λ²)/t²)M, and with −cos²θ + 1 this gives 2 sin²θ − 2μ sin θ/t. The next display uses e^{i(t cos θ)+iμθ}, consistent with the + sign. A numerical check agrees: at μ = 0.4+0.2i, s = 0.9+0.3i, θ = 0.8, t = 1.4, h″ + (1 + (1/4−λ²)/t²)h equals the right side with e^{+i t cos θ} to 12 digits, and differs from it with e^{−i t cos θ}. The slip is isolated and affects nothing.
